License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.02425v1 [cs.CL] 01 Oct 2026 Finding the Move Is Not Winning the Game: XiangqiBench for Closed-Loop Evaluation of LLM Agents Haoyi Xiong Abstract Static evaluations credit a language model for naming the right move, but an agent must carry a plan through to a verified outcome while an opponent responds. We introduce XiangqiBench , an executable benchmark that measures this difference in Chinese chess: starting from 119 tactical endgames with forced mates supported by engine or checks-only search, an LLM agent must deliver checkmate against an engine defender. An interactive REPL interface separates real moves, state queries, and forward simulation, and we record 8,568 multi-turn trajectories from 12 frontier LLMs under two observation protocols. Three signals that look like competence each overstate closed-loop success. (i) The Conversion Gap : models play the stored reference first move in 26.1% of Sighted trials, yet only 13.9% of these trials end in a win. (ii) The Consistency Gap : the leading model reaches 38.7% pass@3 but only 5.9% pass^3 , winning all three trials on 7 of the 46 positions it ever wins. (iii) The Simulation Gap : 32.3% of accepted simulation calls stop on an illegal move, and in 49.3% of comparable cases the real defender replies differently from the line the agent simulated; self-authored rollouts check legality but cannot anticipate the opponent. Finding the move is not winning the game: agent evaluations should score closed-loop outcomes and report reliability alongside coverage. Introduction Figure 1 : XiangqiBench at a glance. Left: a task instance with the real trajectory overlaid on the initial board (numbered plies; deep red for the agent, charcoal for the defender; curves separate annotations and are not piece paths), tool availability by setting, and the scale of the evaluation. Right: the second Red decision of Gemini 3.1 Pro in Sighted trial 3 on case SQYQ-251, after real plies 1–2 (Appendix G ). The complete pre-simulation think response is shown; simulate then checks three model-specified plies, including an assumed Black reply, on a copy of the board. The defender’s actual reply informs the next decision, and the terminal Red win determines task success. Static evaluations such as puzzle solving and move prediction credit a language model for naming a good action ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . Agents are held to a different standard: they must carry a plan through to a verified outcome while an active adversary responds ( Kolasani et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Success then hinges on conversion : navigating an unfolding contingency tree to a verified goal. Whether static competence predicts conversion is rarely measured directly, because existing benchmarks often confound heuristic proposal, mental planning, and closed-loop execution. Board-game endgames provide a controlled testbed for this decision loop: state transitions are exact, legality is executable, and outcomes are determined by verifiable terminal states ( Toshniwal et al., 2022 ; Ruoss et al., 2024 ; Schultz et al., 2025 ) . We study endgame conversion in Chinese chess (Xiangqi): starting from a tactical position in which engine or checks-only search reports a forced mate for Red, an LLM agent plays Red against an engine defender. Agreement with reference moves receives no score; the agent must sustain a winning continuation across multiple turns until checkmate ( Grace et al., 2026 ) . XiangqiBench exposes this process through an interactive Read–Evaluate–Print Loop (REPL) interface (Fig. 1 ) that separates real moves, state queries of the current board and legal moves, and a forward-simulation sandbox on a cloned board. Simulation is not an external search engine: the agent must supply both its own candidate moves and the hypothesized opponent replies. The tool therefore shows what the agent expects: does it anticipate the defender’s replies, or does it check lines the real defender does not play? We evaluate 12 frontier LLMs (Gemini 3.1 Pro ( Google DeepMind, 2026 ) , GPT-5.5 ( OpenAI, 2026 ) , Qwen 3.7 Max ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) , Claude Opus 4.7 ( Anthropic, 2026 ) , DeepSeek V4 Pro/R1/V3.2 ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) , Seed 2.0 Pro ( Seed, 2026 ) , Kimi K2.5 ( Team et al., 2026 ) , Mistral Large 3 ( Mistral AI, 2025 ) , MiniMax M2.5 ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , and GPT-OSS 120B ( Agarwal et al., 2025 ) ; Appendix B ) under two observation settings: Sighted , which provides board refreshes, legal-move feedback, and the simulation sandbox; and Restricted observation , which withholds board refreshes, state queries, and simulation to probe state tracking from move history. Our contributions are: • A benchmark for adversarial conversion: 119 search-supported tactical endgames, an executable rules environment with an engine defender, and 8,568 recorded trajectories. • An instrumented decision loop: we trace each trial from the first move through simulation legality and real-move adoption to defender divergence and the terminal outcome. • Three gaps between apparent and closed-loop competence: a Conversion Gap (the reference first move rarely leads to a win), a Consistency Gap (pass@3 far exceeds pass^3 ), and a Simulation Gap (self-authored rollouts often break legality and mispredict the defender); a controlled ablation on the two strongest models suggests that much of the Restricted-observation drop reflects the setting’s prompt and feedback rather than the missing board alone. Related Work Interactive agent evaluation. AgentBench, SWE-bench, WebArena, and OSWorld evaluate sequential tool invocation and computer control ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) . In game domains, GTBench, GameBench, GAMEBoT, KORGym, and TextArena provide rule-grounded strategic environments ( Duan et al., 2024 ; Costarelli et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2025 ; Guertler et al., 2025 ) . XiangqiBench complements them by isolating adversarial conversion of search-supported winning positions against an engine defender, scoring only the terminal outcome while recording intermediate planning and real-move commitment ( Grace et al., 2026 ) . Game planning, state tracking, and simulation. Board games serve as testbeds for neural planning and representation ( Toshniwal et al., 2022 ; Feng et al., 2023 ; Ruoss et al., 2024 ; Schultz et al., 2025 ) . In chess, ChessArena and LLM Chess evaluate full games against other LLMs, random players, and engines, and ChessArena adds a blindfold mode that supplies only the move history ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Kolasani et al., 2025 ) . LMRL-Gym uses theoretical endgames as a multi-turn RL testbed ( Abdulhai et al., 2025 ) , while Xiangqi-R1 trains a 7B model in multiple stages to improve move legality and position analysis ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . We instead study generalist frontier LLMs on multi-turn endgame conversion and separate the decision loop into scratchpad simulation, real-move adoption, and resilience against engine counterplay. Reliability metrics. Following Chen et al. (2021) and Yao et al. (2025) , we use unbiased finite-sample estimators for pass@ k k (at least one success) and pass^k (all k k attempts succeed); contrasting them reveals whether an agent that can reach a win also reaches it reliably. XiangqiBench: Task Construction Corpus. XiangqiBench curates 119 tactical compositions from classical Chinese-chess treatises in which Red can force checkmate: 116 from Shi Qing Ya Qu 1 1 1 https://www.xqipu.com/canjugupu/1547 (case identifiers SQYQ- n n ) and 3 from the classical Jianghu collection (JH- n n ). Each entry specifies an initial position in Forsyth–Edwards Notation (FEN) with Red to move; historical solution text is withheld from prompts and scoring. During evaluation, an executable rules adapter verifies every proposed action. Xiangqi legality involves non-local constraints: pieces must respect palace boundaries and river crossings, cannons require an intervening screen to capture, horses are blocked by adjacent pieces (“hobbling the horse’s leg”), and generals cannot face each other across an open file. Search-supported admission. Historical treatises can contain transcription errors or overlooked defenses, so source solutions are not trusted. Instead, each position is screened with Pikafish ( Official Pikafish Contributors, 2026 ) , a strong open-source Xiangqi engine derived from Stockfish that combines alpha–beta search with an NNUE evaluation network. For admission , a single-threaded, time-limited search is run from each position, and the position is admitted when the engine reports a forced mate for Red. The reported mate distance and the engine’s preferred first move are stored as case metadata; the latter serves as the reference root move in Section 5 . Composed positions that the engine does not confirm may instead be admitted by a checks-only mate search and are labelled separately (Appendix A ). For defense , the same engine family plays Black during evaluation (Section 4 ). Because admission relies on bounded search rather than a complete proof tree, we describe the positions as search-supported rather than formally proved; all 119 positions were additionally checked manually to confirm that Red can force checkmate. Figure 2 : Stored mate distances of the 119 positions, by category. Distances are those reported at admission by Pikafish or the checks-only solver, stacked by category: 106 threat races (Black would also have a forced mate if it were to move) and 13 unopposed mates (no such counter-mate found). Distances are admission metadata, not limits on trajectory length during evaluation. Why endgames. Like the chess-endgame task in LMRL-Gym ( Abdulhai et al., 2025 ) , we start from endgames rather than full games: the goal (checkmate) is fixed and reachable, so a failure to mate is attributable to the agent; opening recall and attrition are removed; and a few precisely calculated moves decide the game. Unlike LMRL-Gym’s few-piece theoretical endgames against a 1200-Elo engine, ours are composed tactical endgames (median 14 pieces) built on consecutive checks, mating threats, and pins, and a strong engine defends them, so wins cannot rely on blunders. Position categories and horizon. Red can force mate in every position; the two categories differ only in Black’s counterplay. At admission, the same engine or solver is also run with Black to move. If Black then has a forced mate of its own, the position is a threat race : Red must keep forcing, because a slow move can let Black execute its mate first. Otherwise it is an unopposed mate : no counter-mate was found, so a slow move forfeits tempo but does not by itself hand Black a win. Stored mate distances range from 3 to 11 plies (median 9; Figure 2 ). The 40-ply cap is more than three times the longest stored distance, leaving room for detours and recovery, and success already falls steeply within this range (Section 5 ); longer compositions would push nearly every model to zero, whereas this range still separates the strongest models. Interaction and Evaluation Protocol REPL action space. The agent plays Red against an engine defender for at most 40 plies. At each turn it receives an observation o t o_{t} (with interaction history h t h_{t} ) and emits free text alongside a command from three classes (Table 1 ): transitions 𝒜 env \mathcal{A}_{\text{env}} , which commit a move in ICCS coordinates (e.g., move h2h9 ) and trigger the defender’s reply, or resign; read-only queries 𝒜 query \mathcal{A}_{\text{query}} , which inspect the board, legal moves, or history without advancing the game; and hypotheses 𝒜 sim \mathcal{A}_{\text{sim}} , where simulate plays an alternating line of up to 8 model-supplied plies on a cloned board and reports its legality, and think records deliberation. Table 1 : REPL action space and observability contract. Only 𝒜 env \mathcal{A}_{\text{env}} mutates the real board. Class Command & Operational Semantics Sighted Restricted 𝒜 env \mathcal{A}_{\text{env}} (Transitions) move(from_to) : Validate and commit a real move; trigger defender ✓ ✓ resign() : Surrender; terminate trial with defender win ✓ ✓ 𝒜 query \mathcal{A}_{\text{query}} (Perception) view_board() : Render ASCII board, FEN, active color, and piece census ✓ ✗ get_legal_moves() : Enumerate legal moves in the current state ✓ ✗ get_history() : Return the move sequence with piece annotations ✓ ✓ 𝒜 sim \mathcal{A}_{\text{sim}} (Hypothesis) simulate(moves) : Execute alternating line on cloned state; verify legality ✓ ✗ think(text) : Record uncommitted deliberation ✓ ✓ Observation settings. Under Sighted observation, the agent receives the updated board, FEN, and legal moves after every environment step and may use all queries and the simulator; this tests the agent as a system with external perception. Under Restricted observation , the board and FEN are shown once at the start; afterwards the agent receives only move coordinates and captures, view_board , get_legal_moves , and simulate are disabled, and it must track the position from the move history. The two settings also use different system prompts (Appendix A.3 ). Engine defense and termination. After each accepted agent move, Black replies with a fixed-depth (depth-18), single-threaded Pikafish ( Official Pikafish Contributors, 2026 ) search; environment fallbacks are described in Appendix A . A trial ends in an agent win if Red achieves checkmate or leaves Black without legal moves (stalemate is a loss for the stalemated player). It ends in failure upon Black checkmate, agent resignation, exhausting the 40-ply budget, exceeding 3 consecutive illegal moves, or threefold repetition. Under official rules, perpetual checking loses; our replay adjudicates perpetual checks with a simplified long-check rule (Appendix A.5 ). Metrics: exploration vs. consistency. Evaluation Results Figure 3 : Multi-turn endgame conversion across frontier LLMs. Bars report mean pass@1 (single-trial success), pass@3 (at least one success in 3 attempts), and pass^3 (all 3 attempts successful) across 119 positions (357 trials per model/setting). Whiskers denote 95% case-clustered bootstrap intervals. The Consistency Gap: Occasional Success vs. Reliable Conversion Single-trial conversion (pass@1) is low for every model and observation setting (Figure 3 ). Under Sighted observation, Gemini 3.1 Pro leads at 22.1% pass@1 (79/357 trials), followed by GPT-5.5 at 9.0% (32/357) and Qwen 3.7 Max at 6.2% (22/357). Under Restricted observation every model declines: Gemini to 14.0%, GPT-5.5 to 3.4%, and Qwen to 2.8%, with nine models at most 0.8%. Repeated attempts separate reaching a win from reproducing it. For Gemini 3.1 Pro under Sighted observation, pass@3 is 38.7% (46/119 positions) but pass^3 is 5.9% (7/119): of the 46 positions it wins at least once, it wins all three trials on only 7. For GPT-5.5 the corresponding counts are 21 and 3 positions (17.6% and 2.5%). pass^3 is zero in both settings for five models, and zero under Restricted observation for nine. Wins are also not spread evenly over positions. If Gemini’s 22.1% per-trial rate held on every position independently, pass@3 would be 52.7% and pass^3 1.1%; the observed 38.7% and 5.9% indicate that wins concentrate on a subset of positions. Under Sighted observation, Mistral Large 3 and MiniMax M2.5 each win one position in all three trials and no other. Within the subset, outcomes vary from attempt to attempt: on the 46 positions Gemini wins at least once, it wins 57% of trials (79/138), and its split of 20, 19, and 7 positions with one, two, and three wins is close to the 16, 21, and 9 expected from independent trials at that rate. Competence is thus position-specific, and even where it exists a single run does not reveal it reliably. Figure 4 : Deconstructing the Conversion Gap. (a) Mean pass@1 across the 12 LLMs by stored mate distance, per observation setting (95% case-bootstrap intervals; the 3-ply bin contains a single position). (b) Win rate conditioned on whether the agent’s first move matches the stored reference move. The Conversion Gap: Finding the Move vs. Winning the Game Success falls steeply with the stored mate distance (Figure 4 a): Sighted pass@1, averaged over the 12 LLMs, is 11.1% at 5 plies, 6.1% at 7, 2.9% at 9, and 1.8% at 11. The 85 positions at 9 and 11 plies make up 71% of the benchmark. To locate where conversion breaks down, we compare the agent’s first real move with the engine’s stored reference move (Figure 4 b). Across all Sighted trials, the first move matches the reference in 26.1% of cases, far above the 3.3% expected from choosing uniformly among legal root moves; Gemini 3.1 Pro agrees in 45.1% of trials and GPT-5.5 in 42.9%. A correct first move, however, rarely leads to a win. Trials that begin with the reference move are won only 13.9% of the time (155/1,117), so more than 86% of them are lost later in the game. Trials that begin with any other accepted move are won in 0.8% (Sighted) and 0.3% (Restricted observation); a different first move is not necessarily losing, since some positions may admit more than one winning first move. The reference move is thus close to necessary in practice (155 of the 178 Sighted wins begin with it) but far from sufficient. The same gap holds within models: Gemini agrees with the reference move in 45.1% of trials but converts 22.1%; GPT-5.5 agrees in 42.9% but converts 9.0%. We call this the Conversion Gap : an evaluation that scored only the first move would credit these models with roughly two to five times the success they achieve over the full game. The Effect of Restricted Observation Restricted observation lowers pass@1 for every model. Mean pass@1 drops from 4.15% in Sighted to 1.82% in Restricted observation, a reduction of 2.33 percentage points (95% case-bootstrap interval [1.42, 3.41]), or more than half. First-move agreement falls to 15.1%, and the mean rate of terminal invalid-action or no-command losses rises from 2.7% to 27.6% of trials (Section 6 ). Restricted observation, however, also changes the prompt. An ablation that fixes the prompt and removes the state refreshes and the commands separately (Appendix E ) shrinks the drop: on positions they solved under Sighted, GPT-5.5 and Gemini without either win 38.1% and 41.7% of trials, against 39.7% and 48.3% with both and 9.5% and 20.0% under Restricted observation. The drop thus measures the full setting, not the missing board alone. Behavioral Analysis How Models Use the REPL Interface Figure 5 : Action mix by model. Each cell gives the share (%) of all agent REPL calls over complete trajectories spent on each command of Table 1 ; simulate includes budget-rejected calls, move counts accepted moves, and rejected counts rejected moves and the other rejected calls of Figure 6 . Rows sum to 100%. Hatched cells are commands unavailable under Restricted observation. Red numbers give pass@1 (%). Figure 5 shows how each model distributes its actions across the REPL commands; three regularities emerge. Simulation volume does not track success. Under Sighted observation, simulate accounts for 45% of Gemini 3.1 Pro’s actions, but also for 44% of DeepSeek V3.2’s and 43% of DeepSeek V4 Pro’s, whose pass@1 is 0.3% and 2.8%. Seven of the 12 models request simulation in at least 290 of their 357 Sighted trajectories (Table 8 ); only DeepSeek R1 (1.1% of actions) and GPT-OSS 120B (5.0%) largely forgo it. Line length does not separate the models either: Qwen 3.7 Max and Mistral Large 3 request the longest lines (mean 4.2 and 3.9 plies), whereas GPT-5.5 simulates a single ply in 71.9% of accepted calls (Table 9 ). Line legality separates the extremes but not the middle: GPT-5.5 and Gemini obtain at least one fully legal line in 353/356 and 299/332 simulating trajectories, against 14/213 for Mistral Large 3, yet DeepSeek V3.2 reaches 292/352 and still converts almost nothing. Explicit state queries are rare and not concentrated in the strongest models. Because the Sighted interface already returns the board and legal moves after every step, the two strongest models almost never call view_board or get_legal_moves (at most 2.2% of actions); the heaviest users are DeepSeek V3.2 (12% and 8.4%) and DeepSeek V4 Pro (8.6% and 5.8%). Rejected actions dominate the weakest models under Restricted observation. Without state refreshes, rejected actions remain at 5–9% of actions for Gemini, GPT-5.5, and Claude Opus 4.7, rise to 24–42% for the middle group, and reach 93% for Mistral Large 3 and 79% for MiniMax M2.5 (Figure 5 ). These two models contribute 2,101 of the 5,850 Restricted rejections and recover from under 5% of them, whereas Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, and Qwen 3.7 Max recover from at least 88% in both settings (Appendix Figure 19 ; temporal patterns in Section 6.2 ).
